en: Praise of the Teaching;
Homage to the Buddha.
Having approached you for refuge— the Teacher of the World, free from all faults, a mine of virtues, and the peerless King of Physicians— a person who is eternally afflicted [with disease]...
I confess the transformation caused by my own faults. ||1||
Like two rivers with currents difficult to cross,
surging with waves of ill-considered thoughts and reflections, and teeming with a flood of the ocean of the afflictions.
Even in my own mind, there is no peace for me. ||2||
If I were to take refuge in the raft of foulness within the ocean of passion, crowded with its great waves,
it would burn him up there like a dry thicket.
The fire of hatred destroys my mind. ||3||
If I cultivate a mind of loving-kindness for the sake of pacifying the torment of the fire of hatred,
therein [I shall find] that which is cherished by the happiness of all beings.
The mind plunges into the mire of attachment. ||4||
If I were to wash that [body], soiled by the mud of grease, for the sake of purification with indifference,
then how could I not wash the body of the Tathāgata, who removes the suffering of the entire world?
Even the compassion of the Lord of the World diminishes. ||5||
O Lord, if I cultivate compassion,
great weariness arises within me; if I resort to sympathetic joy for its pacification, [the same occurs].
The mind becomes uplifted and restless. ||6||
If, when stirred toward the pacification of joy, the mind becomes sluggish and despondent,
it should be led to exaltation through exertion.
It falls within the range of the enemy that is the conceited man. ||7||
For him, all emptiness is like an enemy; therein his regard for the welfare of others is stilled.
If he were to adopt conventional reality for the sake of others' welfare, [he would act].
Therein the mind shines forth with the desire for wealth. ||8||
The mind has been diminished in its pursuit of acquiring wealth,
made to drink the intoxicant of every vice, and deluded by the sleep of the infatuation of pride.
And indeed, everything that was desired has been destroyed. ||9||
Even when my mind desires to give,
it is overwhelmed by powerful envy;
yet, having shaken that off, if indeed the gift is given—
Then one suffers for a long time. ||10||
If, moreover, that which has been purified by faith falls as a fruit in the next world,
it is rendered free from longing through the perception of impermanence.
Lacking the signless, he becomes indolent and despondent. ||11||
O Lord, although you seek the welfare of others, you behold the world— though it has been a kinsman in all births— as being tormented by extreme suffering.
It is devoured helplessly by the notion of a self.
Following the view of a self, the ego-sense creates the grasping of "mine";
therein arise pride, intoxication, passion, and the rest.
They afflict him like enraged enemies. ||13||
Then, like a terrifying army of Māra, the net of afflictions rose up on all sides,
and the night of the dark fortnight expanded.
Then she was as terrible as the Night of Doom. ||14||
I know that evil is unbearable in its remorse and cruel in its transformation from suffering to birth; yet I myself still commit it.
What indeed could be more painful than this? Or even greater? ||15||
If the mind, which is the cause of manifold sufferings, has been restrained from harming others,
yet it is agitated by the harshness of sword-leaves—
By wicked people who are enemies through their lack of malice. ||16||
Even when my mind desires to be patient, it is bound by the fetters of resentment; therefore,
it is agitated and concentrated upon its own suppression.
Harsh due to being completely parched by the fire of hatred. ||17||
Just as birds avoid a tree whose hollows are infested with the venom of fierce serpents,
so too do they avoid one who conceals the agitation of resentment.
The wise avoid my intention. ||18||
Like stone scorched by the rays of the sun,
like parched and dusty ash,
or like a path thick with sand and dust.
The rain of Dharma has been fruitless within my heart. ||19||
He who, disregarding his own terrible suffering, has exerted himself as if for his own benefit,
being the supreme benefactor through patience and generosity—
O Lord of the World, I cannot endure even that. ||20||
Even while being hostile, fleeing, quivering, or causing pain,
such a person teaches incessantly.
Nor does a teacher appear to me who is like me. ||21||
Having attained that which is difficult to find and worthy of prayer—
the supreme festival of obtaining patience—
if one who possesses the virtue of patience does not indeed endure, [what is the point?]
What other cause for patience do I have?
Beholding the world seized by the rākṣasa of the afflictions, agitated, feverish, disregarding its own welfare, and incapable of looking [at the truth], [the Bodhisattva...]
O Lord, my very hatred is compassion for you. ||23||
I know that every person is subject to their own karma, a vessel for its fruit, powerless and perishable;
yet I imagine another to be the perpetrator of the offense.
Behold the manifestation of the darkness of delusion! 24.
O Lord, I am an ocean of faults and cannot endure even a trace of fault in anyone;
for I am unable to forgive even the excellence of others' virtues.
I cannot endure this supreme wonder. || 25 ||
Like masses of clouds rising on all sides during the rainy season, the multitudes of afflictions repeatedly bring about a gathering within my mind.
Shame on the waters, which are shameless and sluggish! 26.
I am able, if by means of meditative concentration I can conquer with power the arisen web of afflictions,
though the darkness of sloth and torpor now yawns.
And his longing for beds and seats increases. ||27||
The mind, rendered helpless by the noose of passion,
scorched by hatred, and shattered by pride,
[is pierced] by all the arrows, spears, and javelins of the defects.
While practicing, one becomes utterly bewildered on all sides. ||28||
Having bound that which has attained the notion [of self], it remains there;
it trembles, is struck down, and desponds,
deceived by illusion and by deceit.
Distraught, he wanders within the domain of Māra. ||29||
Whatever the object of calm abiding may be, whenever the mind is repeatedly fixed upon it,
it is then no longer helpless under the snares of the afflictions.
It is dragged away by the ropes of greed for sense-objects. ||30||
It brings forth energy that has arisen, and it abandons that which has become agitated; thus, lethargy arises.
For such a person, the application of balanced effort is difficult to attain.
What can my agitated mind do? ||31||
When one practices with wisdom, there arises agitation;
when one resorts to concentration, there arises dullness.
For such a person, the state of the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha) is difficult to attain.
What can my agitated mind do? ||32||
If one carries [the mind] with effort when it has become excited, it becomes dull; then depression arises.
This middle path is difficult to find.
What can my agitated mind do? ||33||
Though the forest of faults is repeatedly scorched by the forest fires of meditative concentration,
its firm root— the view of a self— remains firmly planted.
It sprouts forth on all sides, like [a plant] during the rainy season. ||34||
Even though that [continuum] ceases for one who perceives the continuum as consisting merely of the fruits of afflictions and karma,
the mental continuum itself is also abandoned.
The exertion for the sake of the world is indeed far off. ||35||
The mental continuum of a yogin who is devoid of even a trace of affection and who proceeds with indifference toward all sentient beings attains extinction.
Like the continuity of a lamp, [it ceases] through the exhaustion of the substratum. ||36||
The thought of awakening is the nectar, the elixir that destroys the suffering of the entire world;
it is the cause of enlightenment, cultivated through non-conceptualization.
In that regard, it is only conceptual construction that runs for me. ||37||
Even while contemplating that nothing whatsoever in the world can be grasped by anyone, as if it were a dream-form, I move within the sphere of sensory experience.
[He is] the enemy of the conceptual constructions of the object of awakening and the awakener. ||38||
O Lord, bestow upon me your stainless gaze; behold this most dreadful slaughter,
wherein my very conception of essence is found.
That very thing dissolves right before one's eyes. ||39||
What can the Blessed One do here, or rather,
it is surely my own fault committed in a previous life;
for the sun is the dispeller of the darkness of the entire world.
It dispels the blindness of blinding darkness. ||40||
Of one who has indulged in long-term causes,
whose mind there remains incessantly deluded,
and who is a leper with shriveled hands and feet.
What can a medicine do that has been administered only once? ||41||
The tree of the mind, which has existed since beginningless time and is permeated by the sprinkling of the bitter flavor of the afflictions,
cannot be brought to a state of sweetness.
What are the droplets of the water of virtue? ||42||
My mind, though consisting entirely of all defects,
has become a wondrous elixir of enlightenment;
that very same [mind] has been transformed into a multitude of virtues.
Having brought about the state of fault, it remains. ||43||
Whatever great medicine is prescribed, that very thing turns into poison within me;
for indeed, right method alone is the supreme elixir.
And that [cessation] does not exist; if it does not exist, there is no liberation. ||44||
That which burns away the fullness of the humors,
yet does not provoke another humor,
is what I consider to be the proper method.
"What kind [it is]?"—there is no further determination. ||45||

For those who meditate upon the cultivation of that instruction, [there is] the latent disposition, the underlying tendency, the element, and the habitual impression, which are joined with causes of fault through misconception.
Peace will come here before long. ||46||
For you, the Protector who is free from all faults and who knows the ultimate truth of all phenomena,
even that which has a variegated form is determined to be formless.
It removes the turbidity of all defects. ||47||
Furthermore, for those beholding this form standing before you, radiant with beautiful marks,
it is a drink for the eyes; and for those hearing it, it is nectar for the ears.
The entire web of afflictions is completely shattered. ||48||
Furthermore, O Lord, that unsurpassed sun of the Dharma-body, which is even further beyond,
does not arise for the worlds even when contemplated.
And it indeed destroys cataracts; that is truly marvelous. ||49||
Established in calm abiding (śamatha) wherever it may be,
with whatever supreme mind one possesses, one should act in such a way as to bring happiness to the entire world.
Whoever you are, O Blessed One, whoever you are— homage be to you! By me, whose self is defiled by every fault,
[this has been spoken] before you, who are free from all faults.
Your own accumulation of impurities and sins has been confessed;
therefore, you are the Teacher of the World and the Supreme Lord. ||51||
By whatever merit has been acquired by me here, may [all beings], endowed with the glory of victory over Māra,
attain the path consisting of meditative cultivation.
May embodied beings attain the enlightenment of a Buddha. ||52||
The *Deśanāstava* is completed.
This work is by the venerable Candragomin.
